For over 1,00,000 years, Homo Sapiens warred with the Neanderthals for supremacy — a battle
to the death, literally. Eventually, the early modern humans won out, and Neanderthals went
extinct. And that was the only story ever told. But in these millennia of co-existence, conflict
and competition weren’t the only way the two species engaged with each other. They shared
DNA, 99.7 per cent of it, practices like burying their dead, wearing jewellery, making art —
and families. A new study from the University of Oxford substantiates this claim: Humans and
Neanderthals were in love too, not just at war.


The researchers, studying the evolutionary history of kissing across species, came up with a
simple explanation for a shared oral microbe between Neanderthals and humans. Coupled with
evidence of interbreeding as late as 50,000 years ago, the researchers argue that not only did
Neanderthals, like chimps, bonobos and humans, kiss each other — but human beings too.
There has been a focus on competition — and not nearly enough on cooperation. Robert Ardrey
and Raymond Dart’s “killer ape theory” posited that war and interpersonal aggression was the
driving force behind human evolution. While cooperative competition is part of the history of
survival, this hardly tells the whole story. For instance, bonobos, along with chimps, the closest
evolutionary cousins of Homo Sapiens, privilege cooperation. Like humans, they live in
communities and their tools of choice are affection, negotiation and loyalty. In a world riveted
on differences and obsessed with the rat race, it may help to get better at love, not war.

'I suppose you will be getting away pretty soon, now Fall term is over, Professor,' said a person
not in the story to the Professor of Ontography, soon after they had sat down next to each other
at a feast in the hospitable hall of St James's College. The Professor was young, neat, and
precise in speech.


'Yes,' he said; 'my friends have been making me take up golf this term, and I mean to go to the
East Coast - in point of fact to Burnstow - (I dare say you know it) for a week or ten days, to
improve my game. I hope to get off tomorrow.'


'Oh, Parkins,' said his neighbour on the other side, 'if you are going to Burnstow, I wish you
would look at the site of the Templars' preceptory, and let me know if you think it would be
any good to have a dig there in the summer.'


'Certainly,' said Parkins, the Professor: 'if you will describe to me whereabouts the site is, I will
do my best to give you an idea of the lie of the land when I get back; or I could write to you
about it, if you would tell me where you are likely to be.'


'Don't trouble to do that, thanks. It's only that I'm thinking of taking my family in that direction
in the Long, and it occurred to me that, as very few of the English preceptories have ever been
properly planned, I might have an opportunity of doing something useful on offdays.'

There is more to home advantage than just the pitch. But by asking for specific kinds of wickets,
coach Gautam Gambhir and the India team management have suffered the ignominy of trying
to set a trap for the opposition, and then falling into it themselves. The defeat against South
Africa at Eden Gardens is India’s fourth loss in six home Tests — an indication of how poorly
India, under Gambhir, have played their cards. The last four losses before the most recent
downturn spanned seven years (February 2017 to January 2024). Now, we have seen four in
13 months.


Curators know local conditions best, and if left alone, they will usually try to produce a wicket
that promises good cricket. But when you start asking them to mix things up just a few days
before the game, there is a risk of things backfiring as they did at Eden. The batters, as the Test

tour of England in June-August showed, are good enough, but if you reduce batting to a lottery,
then there are no guarantees. Yes, the batters should have done better. But this is also a young
batting unit that must be allowed to come into its own. Even the best Indian batters have
struggled at home in the last five years — with only Yashasvi Jaiswal (1,322 runs at 57.47)
averaging over 50. A doctored pitch is the last thing such a line-up needs.


Eden Gardens saw great crowds for its first Test in six years, but the match itself ended within
three days. The demand for such pitches, thus, does a disservice to spectators and the game
itself. The England series was fun because it tested the cricketers’ technique and temperament,
and most matches went the distance. India have much to introspect — in terms of both team
and pitch — and it would be a pity if an anticipated win in the next test sweeps these concerns
under the carpet.

India, along with other key markets like China and Brazil, will see a key ingredient in weight
loss drugs go off patent next year. This could lead to a drastic drop in prices as generics makers
ready plans to produce their own versions of these drugs in countries with high incidence of
obesity and associated lifestyle diseases such as diabetes. Competition is intensifying among
patent holders Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk as the expiry approaches. They are trying to shore
up market shares through aggressive price cuts, although these are unlikely to match the level
of inexpensive generics, which could sell for as little as a tenth of current prices.


The strategy is to pitch the drugs at affluent patients as a lifestyle product despite them being
available only by prescription. MNCs holding patents for anti-obesity drugs are also sealing up
arrangements with local pharmaceutical companies to widen their distribution. The idea is to

raise product awareness in price-sensitive markets with rapid growth in obesity so that the
overall numbers make up for market share that will eventually be lost to generics. Effort is also
being made to highlight the innovators' value proposition to physicians. Some combinations
will continue to enjoy patent protection for a while longer.


Affordable slimming drugs are expected to be wildly popular in a country that is battling its
bulge unsuccessfully. A combination of rising affluence and inadequate health awareness
makes India a key market for anti-obesity pills, even if they are not sold over the counter. Some
degree of caution may be called for by Indian drug makers eagerly anticipating a blockbuster
pill going off-patent. There is restraint built into the production process - these drugs are not
easy to replicate. But regulators may have to consider more proactive messaging that while
drugs to lose weight may be within reach, there is no substitute for exercise. The morning walk
will do you more good than popping a pill to confuse your brain about hunger. But that's
another ask and task.

Since the advent of Bitcoin, and the subsequent proliferation of cryptocurrencies, there have
been concerns over the regulatory challenges posed by the crypto universe. Over the years,


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                      10

12 Minutes to CLAT                                                  CLAT 2027 Mock Test - 27


numerous instances of fraud, scams and other illicit activities have come to light. For instance,
in 2022, FTX, a cryptocurrency exchange, collapsed, and its founder Sam Bankman-Fried was
convicted for fraud and conspiracy to launder money. In 2023, Changpeng Zhao, founder of
Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, pleaded guilty to violating US anti-money
laundering laws. Crypto exchanges have been levied fines, penalties, and settlements totalling
more than $5.8 billion, according to an analysis by the International Consortium of
Investigative Journalists (ICIJ). In India, between 2024 and 2025, the Financial Intelligence
Unit has levied fines on Binance (Rs 18.82 crore), ByBit (Rs 9.27 crore) and KuCoin (Rs 34.5
lakh) — for violating anti-money laundering laws. Crypto regulation is fragmented. Taking
advantage of this grey zone, crypto exchanges have become hubs for dirty money to cross
national borders as shown by an investigation by this paper, in partnership with the ICIJ. This
is a matter of grave concern.


A shadow economy has emerged worldwide, and India is no exception. The anonymity that
crypto offers along with the ease of transferring across borders makes this a widely preferred
medium. For instance, following the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the World Economic Forum
noted concerns about the use of crypto to evade international sanctions. In addition to hawala
deals, even money stolen by cybercrimes is being channelled through these routes — as per an
estimate, Rs 623 crore has been funneled.


India, with more than 100 million users, is a big crypto market. However, there is no
overarching crypto framework that regulates the sector. Crypto exchanges, wallet providers
and others must register with the Financial Intelligence Unit. But those who have done so
account for only a small proportion of the universe. As this space grows — from $2.6 billion
to $15 billion by 2035, as per an estimate — there is need for policy clarity. The guardrails
need to be put in place.

Offences against property in the Indian Penal Code, now mirrored in the Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita, operate along a graduated scale of severity. Extortion, robbery, and dacoity form a
connected chain, with each successive offence incorporating the elements of the one before it
and adding a further aggravating ingredient.

Extortion, under the IPC, is constituted by three cumulative elements: the accused must
intentionally put a person in fear of injury, that fear must be induced so as to cause the person
to deliver property or a valuable security, and the delivery must be in consequence of that fear.
The fear need not be of bodily harm; a threat to injure reputation or to cause wrongful loss to



                                   12minutestoclat.com                                        20

12 Minutes to CLAT                                                   CLAT 2027 Mock Test - 27


any person in whom the threatened party is interested suffices. Crucially, no immediate
confrontation is required — the threat may be communicated remotely, and the offence is
complete the moment the person parts with the property out of apprehension, whether or not
the accused is physically present.

Robbery is defined as theft or extortion in an aggravated form. Theft becomes robbery when,
in order to commit theft, or in carrying away or attempting to carry away property, the offender
voluntarily causes or attempts to cause death, hurt, or wrongful restraint to any person, or puts
any person in fear of instant death, instant hurt, or instant wrongful restraint. Extortion becomes
robbery when the offender, at the time of committing the extortion, is present in person and
puts the victim in fear of instant injury. The key distinction from ordinary extortion is the
element of immediacy and the physical presence of the perpetrator.

Dacoity elevates the offence further: it occurs when five or more persons conjointly commit or
attempt to commit robbery. Every person who is one of the five or more persons assembled for
that purpose is deemed to have committed dacoity. This constructive or joint liability rule is
unsparing: a member of the assembly who neither wields a weapon nor participates actively in
the taking is still guilty of dacoity, because the law attributes the collective act to each
participant individually. The rationale is deterrence — the presence of large numbers amplifies
the terror and coercive capacity of the group beyond what any individual could achieve.

Section 494 of the Indian Penal Code, re-enacted as Section 82 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita,
penalises a person who contracts a second marriage during the lifetime of a living spouse,
provided the first marriage subsists and has not been dissolved by a competent court. The
offence is premised on the second marriage being void by reason of the first. This dependency
on voidness is the provision's most critical feature: if the second marriage is not rendered void
by the applicable personal law, the criminal provision is not attracted.

For Muslim males governed by Muslim personal law, the plurality of marriages is permitted,
subject to the conditions of equal treatment and financial capacity recognised by that law. A
second marriage contracted by a Muslim husband is not void under Muslim personal law; it is
treated as legally valid. Because the second marriage is not void, the predicate for the criminal
offence of bigamy under Section 494 IPC or Section 82 BNS is absent, and no prosecution will
lie.

The contrast with Hindu law is stark. Under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, a second marriage
contracted during the subsistence of a first marriage is null and void, regardless of
circumstances. This absolute prohibition makes a Hindu's second marriage the paradigm case
for bigamy under the penal provision.

       BNSS (previously Section 482 CrPC) to quash criminal proceedings may be exercised

Partnership under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 is the relation between persons who have
agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all. This
definition reveals four indispensable elements: an agreement between two or more persons, a
business being carried on, sharing of profits, and mutual agency. Mutual agency is the crucial
structural element: each partner is simultaneously the principal who can be bound by the acts
of co-partners, and the agent who can bind those co-partners. A mere sharing of profits is not,
by itself, conclusive evidence of a partnership; the mutual agency element must be present.

Partners stand in a fiduciary relationship with one another. Each partner is required to be just
and faithful to the firm, to render true accounts, and to account for any private profit derived
from any transaction connected with the firm or from any use of the firm's property or goodwill.
If a partner, without the consent of co-partners, carries on a business of the same nature
competing with that of the firm, that partner must account to the firm for all profits made. These
fiduciary obligations persist throughout the duration of the partnership and bind both active
and dormant partners equally.

Toward third parties, partners bear joint and several liability for all acts of the firm done while
they were partners. A third party who suffers loss may sue any one partner or all of them, and
recovery from one partner does not extinguish the obligations of the rest. Registration of a firm


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                         27

12 Minutes to CLAT                                                     CLAT 2027 Mock Test - 27


does not affect this liability toward outsiders; it does, however, affect the firm's ability to
enforce its own claims in court, as an unregistered firm cannot sue third parties to enforce
contract rights, though this disability does not bar third parties from suing the firm.

When a partner retires, they continue to be liable to third parties for acts of the firm until public
notice of retirement is given. Without such notice, persons who had previously dealt with the
firm may continue to treat the retiring partner as still a member and hold her liable for
subsequent obligations. Dissolution of the firm, by contrast, terminates the firm's existence
entirely, and assets must be applied in a prescribed order: first to discharge liabilities to third
parties, then to repay partners' advances, and finally to return capital contributions, with any
residue shared in the profit-sharing ratio.

The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 established Lok Adalats as a statutory mechanism
for alternative dispute resolution. The framework is tiered: the National Legal Services
Authority operates at the apex, the State Legal Services Authorities function at the state level,
District Legal Services Authorities operate at the district level, and Taluk Legal Services
Committees serve sub-district areas. Each level is empowered to organise Lok Adalats for
disputes falling within its territorial and subject-matter jurisdiction.

Lok Adalats have jurisdiction over two categories of disputes. First, they may take up matters
pending before a court if both parties consent to a reference. Second, they may address pre-
litigation disputes where no court proceedings have been initiated, provided again that both
parties agree to participate. One category of disputes is, however, expressly excluded: offences
that are not compoundable under any law in force cannot be settled before a Lok Adalat. This
restriction reflects the legislative policy that where the State has determined that private
settlement of an offence is impermissible, the Lok Adalat mechanism cannot be used to
circumvent that determination.

Once a Lok Adalat arrives at a settlement, the award it records is deemed to be a decree of a
civil court and is final and binding on the parties. Critically, no appeal lies from a Lok Adalat
award to any court. The only recourse available to a party dissatisfied with the outcome is to
treat the settlement as not having occurred and to pursue the original remedy before the
appropriate forum. This finality, combined with the absence of court fees on Lok Adalat
proceedings, makes it an attractive mode of resolution.

Permanent Lok Adalats are a specialised institution established under Chapter VI-A of the Act
for disputes relating to public utility services, which include transport, insurance, supply of
power, and similar essential services. Unlike ordinary Lok Adalats, a Permanent Lok Adalat is
empowered to impose a settlement on the parties even if one party objects, provided the dispute
relates to a public utility service. This power to make binding determinations without bilateral
consent distinguishes Permanent Lok Adalats structurally from the consensus-based ordinary
Lok Adalat.

The Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 codifies the right of a Hindu wife to claim

independently of, and outside, the HAMA framework. She may claim maintenance dehors the
statute — that is, by invoking her common law rights as recognised and preserved by the courts.

The significance of this ruling lies in its extension to the husband's immovable property. The
court held that a Hindu wife is entitled to claim maintenance directly from her husband's
immovable property, not merely from his personal income or movable assets. Once
proceedings for maintenance are instituted, the wife's right to maintenance attaches as a charge
on the husband's immovable property from the date of initiation of those proceedings. This

The Right to Information Act, 2005 was conceived as a transparency statute, creating a
presumption in favour of disclosure and placing the burden on public authorities to justify
withholding information. Section 8 of the Act contains exemptions from the obligation to
furnish information. Among the most frequently invoked was Section 8(1)(j), which exempted
personal information from disclosure where such information had no nexus with any public
activity or interest, or where its disclosure would cause unwarranted invasion of the privacy of
an individual.

A critical feature of Section 8(1)(j) as originally enacted was the proviso that the Public
Information Officer, or the Central or State Information Commission on appeal, could order
disclosure of personal information if satisfied that the larger public interest justified disclosure.
This proviso operated as a proportionality mechanism: disclosure of otherwise private
information could be compelled if the public benefit of exposure outweighed the individual's
privacy interest. This balance reflected the foundational tension between the right to
information and the right to privacy.

The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 fundamentally altered this equilibrium. Section
44(3) of the DPDPA amended Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act by removing the proviso that had
permitted disclosure in the larger public interest. As a consequence, personal information is
now categorically exempt from disclosure, and no officer or authority retains the power to order
its disclosure on public interest grounds. The proportionality test, which once required a
contextual weighing of competing interests, has been replaced by what amounts to a near-
absolute exemption.

This amendment has attracted considerable commentary from transparency advocates, who
argue that it fundamentally undermines the accountability function of the RTI Act, particularly
in cases where personal information of public officials is sought in connection with their
official conduct. Critics contend that the removal of the public interest override eliminates the
legal basis for disclosing asset declarations, financial relationships, and other information that,
while personal in form, is material to democratic accountability. Supporters of the amendment

argue that it brings the RTI framework into alignment with the stronger privacy protections the
DPDPA is designed to guarantee.
